seats.oldValue: Sends the girl for nails and goes with her.
seats.newValue: Sends the girl out for nails, then he goes after her.
seats.execution: Takes the right sentence but the wrong second half. Line 9 has him send one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; he does not go after her himself.

seats.oldValue: He drops it and the glass stays whole.
seats.newValue: He drops it, the frame comes off, and he does save the glass.
seats.execution: Line 19 says he would try to save the glass, and cut himself. The option drops the 'try' and the cut, and the glass is not saved: lines 24 and 25 say a new glass had been got.

seats.oldValue: Because he goes out of the room to see to his cut.
seats.newValue: Because his tools are in the coat, and nobody knows where the coat is.
seats.execution: Lines 20 and 21 put the handkerchief in the pocket of the coat he had taken off. The tools are what the house leaves off looking for at line 22; the child moves the coat pocket from the handkerchief to the tools.

seats.oldValue: The charwoman's corns.
seats.newValue: The string.
seats.execution: The string is in line 43, but it is what slips, not what he lands on. Lines 43 and 44 have him slide down on to the piano when it slips.

seats.oldValue: Hide the hammer so he cannot start at all.
seats.newValue: Have him stay at his mother's while the job is done.
seats.execution: Lines 49 to 51 have Aunt Maria hope to go and spend a week with her mother while it was being done. The child swaps who goes away, sending Uncle Podger instead of Aunt Maria.

seats.oldValue: He is boasting to them, and hiding it, because it went so badly.
seats.newValue: He is boasting so that nobody will see he knows the job went very badly.
seats.execution: A knowing reading, but line 62 states the pride as real: he surveys the mess with evident pride. No line shows him aware that the job went badly.

seats.oldValue: By pulling the blankets off her bed.
seats.newValue: By pulling her blankets off, one by one.
seats.execution: Pulling the blankets off is a common way to wake someone, but no line in the passage has it. Line 1 says Roberta woke Phyllis by pulling her hair gently.

seats.oldValue: They wash in a basin.
seats.newValue: One of them washes at the basin while the other pumps.
seats.execution: Basin washing is only Roberta's comparison at line 11, outside this window. Lines 9 and 10 have them wash under the spout of the pump in the yard: one pumped and the other washed.

seats.oldValue: They built the fire far too big for the kettle.
seats.newValue: They made the fire far too big, so the kettle burned.
seats.execution: Line 41 calls it an excellent fire, and no line says it was too big. The bottom burns out because the kettle was set on at about half-past five, at line 41, and left there while they sat outside and fell asleep.

seats.oldValue: Because it was a lovely July evening for a drive.
seats.newValue: Because it was a lovely July evening, and they started their drive.
seats.execution: True at lines 2 and 3: they started on their drive, and it was a lovely July evening. Neither is why he sent for anything; line 1 gives the reason, that the nearest railway station is seven miles away.

seats.oldValue: The children had been given the day off school.
seats.newValue: Tom and Maggie were let off school, as a treat.
seats.execution: No school is mentioned anywhere in the passage, let alone a day off as a treat. Lines 1 to 4 give the reason: the scents of plumcakes, jellies and gravy make it impossible to feel altogether gloomy.

seats.oldValue: Tom asks whether Maggie will run away tomorrow.
seats.newValue: Tom asks whether Maggie will run away; she says she will not.
seats.execution: Lines 7 and 8 run the other way: Maggie asks Tom whether he shall run away to-morrow, and Tom answers at lines 9 and 10. The child swaps who asks and who answers.

seats.oldValue: Maggie tells Tom to shut his own eyes and then choose.
seats.newValue: Maggie tells Tom to keep his own eyes shut and choose.
seats.execution: Lines 27 to 31 run the other way: Tom asks Maggie to choose right or left, and tells her to keep her eyes shut. The child swaps who gives the instruction and who obeys it.

seats.oldValue: She gives up the best piece out of pure sacrifice.
seats.newValue: She gives Tom the best bit out of her power of sacrifice.
seats.execution: Line 33 says Maggie's power of sacrifice did not extend so far, and this option loses that not. Lines 33 to 35 give the real reason: she wants Tom pleased with her for giving him the best bit.

seats.oldValue: He was pleased to watch her enjoy her half.
seats.newValue: He watched her, pleased to see her enjoy it.
seats.execution: Line 44 has him watch her feeling in himself a capacity for more, which is appetite rather than pleasure. At line 47 he calls her a greedy thing, so he was not pleased.

seats.oldValue: Because he was jealous of how much she enjoyed it.
seats.newValue: Because he was jealous of how much she enjoyed her half.
seats.execution: Lines 48 and 49 give Tom's reason: he was conscious of having acted very fairly, and thought she ought to have made up to him for it. The child supplies a different motive, jealousy of her pleasure, that the text never supports.

seats.oldValue: That they had driven eight miles that day.
seats.newValue: That they had driven eight miles that very morning.
seats.execution: Lines 25 and 26 have the mother say they drove eight miles that morning. That is outside this window, and it was the child and her mother, not Mr Cobb; lines 3 and 4 say he never lost sight of the fact that he carried the mail.

seats.oldValue: The rattle and rumble of the wheels.
seats.newValue: The rattle of the wheels, or the creaking harness.
seats.execution: Lines 36 and 37 give the rattle and rumble of the wheels and the creaking of the harness as the noise he heard the voice above. The child takes those noises for the answer; line 37 says he first thought it was a cricket, a tree toad, or a bird.

seats.oldValue: The stage is far too small for her.
seats.newValue: The stage is too small, and the windows are too big.
seats.execution: Line 46 says the stage is so much too big for her, and line 47 says the windows are so small. The child swaps the two sizes between the stage and the windows.

seats.oldValue: Smoothed it out with great care.
seats.newValue: Smoothed it out under her as she sat.
seats.execution: Line 53 has her sit down carefully, smoothing her dress under her. That is what she did to her dress; line 54 has her put the sunshade under its extended folds.

seats.oldValue: Mark ran for the rod while the fish waited.
seats.newValue: Mark ran for the rod, but the fish did not wait.
seats.execution: The fish did go at line 6, but lines 3 and 5 have Mark refuse to go for the rod. The child reads Bevis's 'if you had run quick' as if Mark had run, which the lines state the contrary of.

seats.oldValue: Standing up very straight and stiff.
seats.newValue: Stiff, and standing up very straight.
seats.execution: Line 19 gives this manner to Bevis, who marched on very upright. The child moves Bevis's detail onto the sand; line 20 has Mark put his feet into the marks Bevis left in it.

seats.oldValue: The bushes have spread outwards from the shore.
seats.newValue: The bushes have shrunk in the summer heat.
seats.execution: Lines 23 and 24 say it is the lake that has shrunk under the summer heat; the willow bushes have not moved. The child gives the shrinking to the bushes instead of the lake.

seats.oldValue: Pan follows him along once he has set off.
seats.newValue: Pan follows him along the face of the cliff.
seats.execution: Turns the dog into the follower. Lines 52 and 53 have Pan run along the face of the cliff ahead of Bevis, who has only just pushed into the furze.

seats.oldValue: That he wanted the game to end sooner.
seats.newValue: That he did not even get a hand to it.
seats.execution: Lines 26 and 27 say "I could have had it. I had my hands on it." The option claims the contrary of what he says about this goal.

seats.oldValue: That Denise stakes her dahlias too late.
seats.newValue: That Denise does not stake her dahlias early enough.
seats.execution: True at line 7, where Grandad says staked late. It is his remark, not what Cass decides about it; lines 8 and 9 say she did not say so, because it was not that kind of conversation.
